sections.html:
Bryan County is in the Savannah metropolitan area and Fort Stewart cuts it in two. Pembroke, the county seat, sits in the rural north. Richmond Hill, the biggest city, is a Savannah suburb in the south, and a public-road trip between the two leaves the county. That divide is why the county keeps two offices for nearly every property tax service.

The county counted 44,738 people in 2020, and mid-2025 is 52,062, up 16.4 percent from the 2020 base. Homes have a middle value of $343,200 and household income has a middle of $103,408. Builders pulled 733 permits in 2025, and 77.7 percent of housing is owner occupied. The north tends toward larger rural parcels, while the south has newer subdivisions in the Savannah commuter zone.

The assessor and the tax commissioner each run one office in Pembroke and one in Richmond Hill. The assessor sets values. The commissioner handles billing, collection and distribution. The assessor's side neither sets the rate nor collects a dollar.

Commissioner offices keep weekday hours of 8:30 to 5:00 and stay open over lunch. The county's assessor page and commissioner page carry these details. Go to whichever location is closer, since both handle the same tax matters.

This year's bills were mailed October 16 and are due Tuesday, December 15, 2026. In general, bills go out around September and give at least 60 days to pay, so the date can shift from year to year. See the county's property tax page.

Late payment brings these charges:

  • Interest runs at 0.875 percent per month, or fraction of a month, beginning the day after the deadline
  • At 120 days past due, a 5 percent penalty is added
  • Each further 120 days adds another 5 percent, with 20 percent as the ceiling
  • A bill 30 days delinquent lets the tax commissioner, serving as ex-officio sheriff, start tax sale proceedings

Under Georgia law the January 1 owner of record stays on the bill for the year, and the office asks for the recorded deed once a sale closes.

sections.h2: How value is set and how to appeal
sections.html:
The assessor sets fair market value. Forty percent of it, less any homestead exemption, becomes the taxable value, and the commissioner then applies the millage rate. The county posts the current millage rates on its tax page.

Appeals have strict rules, and late appeals are refused. The window is 45 days from the date on the notice:

  • Use the county's written appeal form
  • Get it physically to the Pembroke or Richmond Hill office before 5:00 p.m. on deadline day
  • Nothing sent by email or fax is accepted, and a postmark proves nothing

The assessor's staff photograph homes to refresh records, so a county vehicle may pause outside yours. After a sale, the new owner sees a value the following year, when the first notice arrives.

Questions about a value belong with the assessor at 912-653-3889, option 1. The assessor's page also offers a guide called Understanding Your Notice of Assessment, which walks through each line of the notice. Read it before you decide whether an appeal is worth filing.

sections.h2: Who is billed when a house changes hands
sections.html:
The commissioner does not prorate taxes by the date of sale, by how much the property was used or by who owns it now. Any split between buyer and seller therefore happens at the closing table.

Once you sell, give the tax commissioner the recorded deed and closing papers so the next bill finds the new owner. Leave them at either office, mail them to P.O. Box 447, Pembroke, GA 31321, or email propertytax@bryancountyga.gov. Address changes and homestead applications belong with the assessor.

Find out from your closing attorney how this year's bill will be shared and whether the December deadline lands before your closing. For any open bill, get a payoff figure from the commissioner so it can come out of the sale. A cash buyer who takes the house as is will still expect that figure, and having it in writing keeps the closing on schedule.

sections.h2: Steps for a Bryan County seller
sections.html:
A sale in Bryan County is easier when you handle the paperwork in a set order. Because there are two offices of each kind, pick the one closer to you and stay with it.

  1. Call the tax commissioner and ask for the balance on every account under your name: the house, any mobile home, and any business property.
  2. Check whether the December deadline falls before your closing date, and decide with the buyer who pays.
  3. Request a written payoff for any open bill and give it to the closing attorney.
  4. After closing, deliver the recorded deed so the next bill is mailed to the new owner.
  5. Tell the assessor about any homestead exemption you held, since the buyer must apply separately.

If a bill is already delinquent, move faster. At 30 days past due the commissioner can begin tax sale proceedings, and a sale in progress is far harder to close around than a simple payoff. A call to either office on the same day you get a contract is cheap protection.

sections.h2: Homestead, mobile homes and business property
sections.html:
The county's sample calculation uses a $2,000 homestead reduction from assessed value. Applications go to the assessor, and your status on January 1 decides eligibility, so ask that office which exemptions match your age, income or veteran status.

Mobile homes are billed under their own rules. Without a homestead exemption, the bill arrives in January and is due April 1. With one, the home is taxed along with its land, and that bill is due around November 15. Taxes must be paid, with a receipt in hand, before any mobile home is moved, even out of the county.

A business must file a personal property return with the assessor by April 1 in every year it operates, and state-set values apply if it does not. Timber sales go on Department of Revenue form PT-283T, and heavy-duty equipment bought from a dealer is taxed in its purchase year.

If you own more than one kind of property, ask the commissioner which accounts exist under your name. A forgotten mobile home or business account can hold up a closing just as a missed house bill can.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 due date for Bryan County property tax?
faqs.a: The 2026 bills are due Tuesday, December 15, 2026, and were mailed on October 16. After the due date, interest of 0.875 percent per month applies.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Bryan County assessment?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the date on the notice, in writing, delivered to the Pembroke or Richmond Hill office by 5:00 p.m. on the last day. Late appeals are refused.

faqs.q: Does Bryan County split property tax by sale date?
faqs.a: No. The commissioner's office does not prorate by sale date, so the buyer and seller settle the bill between them at closing.

faqs.q: Where should the deed go after a Bryan County sale?
faqs.a: Send the recorded deed and closing documents to the Bryan County Tax Commissioner, P.O. Box 447, Pembroke, GA 31321, or to propertytax@bryancountyga.gov. You can also drop them at the Pembroke or Richmond Hill office.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay Bryan County property tax?
faqs.a: Interest and penalties accumulate, and penalties stop at 20 percent. Once a bill is 30 days delinquent the commissioner may start tax sale proceedings, so call early if you cannot pay in full.
